title: Tomorrow
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The everyday future is aller plus a BARE infinitive: Je vais manger. English's "going to" is the same idea with a "to" inside it, and that "to" is exactly the word French does not write — Je vais à manger is the interference.
aller is irregular and carries the module: je vais · vous allez · il/elle va. The same verb also does plain movement — je vais à Paris — so one word covers both the plan and the journey.

There is a second future, the futur simple (je mangerai), and this level does not teach it: a plan is aller + infinitive, and the -rai form is what a French speaker reaches for LEAST when making one. "will = the future tense" is the slogan that would send you to the wrong form.

The plain present is a perfectly normal future once a time word has said so: Demain matin je travaille. English can do this too — "I work tomorrow" — so it is the one part of the module that transfers whole.
The negation wraps the verb that carries the person, which here is vais: Je ne vais pas partir. The infinitive stays outside the brackets, exactly as it did in L1-M3 and L1-M5.
Time phrases stand at the front of the sentence or at its end, never in the middle: demain, ce soir, demain matin, la semaine prochaine.
A question is still the statement with a rising voice: Vous allez rester à la maison ?

words.note: tomorrow. It stands at the front of the sentence or at the end and never in the middle, like every time word in this course.
aller, to go — irregular: je vais · vous allez · il/elle va. Two jobs: before a bare verb it makes a plan (je vais travailler); before a place it is plain movement (je vais à Paris).

sentences.trap: English's "going to" carries a "to" that French does not have. Je vais à travailler is the sentence an English speaker assembles, and the à is the one word too many in it.
sentences.sound: duh-MAN zhuh veh tra-va-YAY. demain ends nasal, and vais is one syllable with its -s silent.

variations.display: Demain je vais manger à la maison
variations.cue: Tomorrow I'm going to eat at home
variations.changed: swap the plan — the frame and the time word do not move

variations.cue: Are you going to work tomorrow?
variations.changed: allez for the person spoken to, the time word at the end, and a rising voice

variations.display: Demain je ne vais pas travailler
variations.cue: Tomorrow I'm not going to work
variations.changed: the brackets close round vais; the infinitive stays outside them

mistake.why: Nothing stands between aller and the verb it plans: je vais travailler. The à is English's "to" arriving where French keeps the gap empty.

sentences.usage: The ordinary way to say what you will do.
sentences.mnemonic: "I go work" — French plans by going, and puts nothing in between.

sentences.cue: I'm going to buy some bread

words.note: to buy — the bare form of the verb whose participle L1-M5 taught as acheté. The two are said exactly alike, ash-TAY, so only the page tells them apart: after vais it must be the bare form.

sentences.trap: This is where the homophone starts costing something. j'ai acheté (I bought) and je vais acheter (I'm going to buy) differ in speech only in the little verb at the front — the ending sounds identical in both.
sentences.sound: ash-TAY, with the first syllable barely there. The whole line runs zhuh veh ash-TAY dü pan.

variations.cue: I'm going to buy a car
variations.changed: a countable object — une rather than the partitive

variations.cue: Are you going to buy bread?
variations.changed: allez and a rising voice

variations.cue: Yesterday I bought bread
variations.changed: the same verb pointed backwards: the auxiliary changes and the ending gains its accent

mistake.why: After vais the verb is bare: acheter. acheté is the participle, and it belongs behind j'ai.

sentences.usage: An errand you are about to run.
sentences.mnemonic: -er after vais, -é after j'ai. The ear cannot help; the accent can.

sentences.display: Vous allez rester à la maison ?
sentences.cue: Are you going to stay at home?
sentences.literal: You go stay at the house ?

words.note: to stay — the bare form behind L1-M5's resté. In the past it took être, being on that short list; in a plan it is simply the verb after allez, and no auxiliary is involved at all.

sentences.trap: English needs "are" hauled to the front to ask this. French adds nothing: the statement Vous allez rester à la maison becomes the question by the voice and the mark alone.
sentences.sound: voo-za-lay res-TAY. The -s of vous wakes into a z in front of allez, so the first two words run together.

variations.display: Je vais rester à la maison
variations.cue: I'm going to stay at home
variations.changed: the answer, in the first person — allez becomes vais

variations.cue: Are you going to stay here?
variations.changed: swap the place phrase for a single word

variations.display: Je ne vais pas rester à la maison
variations.cue: I'm not going to stay at home
variations.changed: the brackets close round vais, with rester outside them

mistake.why: Two things: this course asks with a rising voice rather than by inverting, and a question always carries its mark. Vous allez rester à la maison ?

sentences.mnemonic: The verb never moves. The voice does the asking.

sentences.cue: Tomorrow I'm going to see Anne

words.note: to see — the bare form behind L1-M5's vu. Unlike the -er verbs, its bare form and its participle look and sound nothing alike, which for once makes the pair easy to keep apart.

sentences.trap: A person after voir needs no preposition and no article: voir Anne, exactly as English sees Anne. The transfer is complete, and it is worth noticing how rare that is in this module.
sentences.sound: vwar, one syllable, with the r in the back of the throat — the same ending as boire and soir.

variations.display: Ce soir je vais voir Marc
variations.cue: This evening I'm going to see Marc
variations.changed: a different time word at the front, and a different person after the verb

variations.cue: Are you going to see the film?
variations.changed: allez, a rising voice, and a thing rather than a person

variations.cue: Yesterday I saw Anne
variations.changed: the same verb pointed backwards — and the past shape shares nothing with the bare one

mistake.why: vu is the participle and belongs behind j'ai. After vais the verb is bare: voir.

sentences.mnemonic: voir, vu — the only pair in the module you can tell apart by ear.

sentences.cue: This evening I'm going to eat

words.note: this evening. Take the two words together: ce is "this" and is not taught alone here. Note the contrast with L1-M4's le soir — le soir is every evening, a habit; ce soir is the one that is coming.

sentences.trap: le soir and ce soir differ by one small word and mean quite different things: the habit against the single occasion. English marks the same difference with "in the evening" against "this evening", so the distinction transfers even though the words do not.
sentences.sound: suh SWAR — the same soir as in le soir, with ce reduced almost to nothing in front of it.

variations.cue: This evening I'm going to sleep
variations.changed: swap the plan — the time phrase does not move

variations.display: Le soir je mange à la maison
variations.cue: In the evening I eat at home
variations.changed: le rather than ce: a habit rather than one particular evening

variations.cue: Are you going to eat this evening?
variations.changed: allez, a rising voice, and the time phrase moved to the end

mistake.why: soir is masculine, so it is ce soir. cette is the feminine form and belongs in front of a feminine noun.

sentences.usage: A plan for the same day.
sentences.mnemonic: le is the habit, ce is the one in front of you.

sentences.display: Je ne vais pas partir demain
sentences.cue: I'm not going to leave tomorrow
sentences.literal: I not go not leave tomorrow

words.note: to leave — another movement verb that takes être in the past, though here it is simply the bare verb after vais. Its -ir ending marks a third verb family, beside manger's -er and boire's -re.

sentences.trap: The brackets grip vais and nothing else. English would put the "not" next to "leave"; French leaves partir standing entirely outside the negation, exactly as it left the infinitive alone in L1-M3.
sentences.sound: par-TEER, with both r's in the throat. The whole line has six beats and only the last two carry any weight.

variations.cue: I'm going to leave tomorrow
variations.changed: the brackets come away and nothing else changes

variations.cue: Aren't you going to leave tomorrow?
variations.changed: allez inside the same brackets, with ne shortened in front of its vowel

variations.display: Je ne vais pas rester ici
variations.cue: I'm not going to stay here
variations.changed: swap the infinitive — the brackets do not notice

mistake.display: Je vais ne pas partir demain
mistake.why: The brackets go round the verb that carries the person, and that is vais: Je ne vais pas partir.

sentences.mnemonic: The brackets always grip the verb that changed for you.

sentences.display: La semaine prochaine je vais à Paris
sentences.cue: Next week I'm going to Paris
sentences.literal: The week next I go to Paris

words.note: next week — three words, taken whole. Two things inside it: the adjective comes after its noun, as French adjectives usually do, and the definite article is there where English has nothing at all.

sentences.trap: Here vais has no infinitive behind it and is not making a plan at all: it is plain movement, "I go to Paris". The same word, the other of its two jobs — which is why its note had to be written for both.
sentences.sound: la suh-MEN pro-SHEN. Both words end in the same -aine sound, and neither final -e is heard.

variations.display: La semaine prochaine je vais travailler
variations.cue: Next week I'm going to work
variations.changed: an infinitive behind vais — the plan reading, with the same time phrase

variations.cue: Tomorrow I'm going to Paris
variations.changed: a shorter time word; the movement reading is unchanged

variations.cue: Are you going to Paris?
variations.changed: allez and a rising voice, still with no infinitive behind it

mistake.display: La prochaine semaine je vais à Paris
mistake.why: The adjective follows the noun: la semaine prochaine. Putting it in front is English's order arriving whole.

sentences.usage: A plan further out than tomorrow.
sentences.mnemonic: French says the week, then which week.

words.note: tomorrow morning — the two words simply set side by side, with nothing between them. Compare L1-M4's le matin, which needed its article to mean every morning: a specific morning takes none.

sentences.trap: There is no aller here and no future ending either — just the present, made future by the time word in front of it. English does exactly the same thing ("tomorrow morning I work"), so this is the one shape in the module that needs no translating at all.
sentences.sound: duh-MAN ma-TAN. Both words end nasal, and neither n is sounded on its own.

variations.cue: Tomorrow morning I'm going to work
variations.changed: the aller frame instead of the plain present — both are ordinary French

variations.display: Demain matin je bois du café
variations.cue: Tomorrow morning I'm drinking coffee
variations.changed: swap the verb; the present keeps doing the future's work

variations.cue: In the morning I work
variations.changed: le rather than demain: a habit rather than one particular morning

mistake.why: The article belongs to the habit, not to a named morning: demain matin, and le matin only when it means every morning.

sentences.usage: A near, fixed plan — the way a diary entry is said out loud.
sentences.mnemonic: Name the morning and the article goes away.

sentences.cue: This evening I'm going to sleep

words.note: to sleep — another -ir verb, like partir. It is not reflexive, so nothing stands between je and the frame: compare je me lève, where the little pronoun was part of the verb.

sentences.trap: English has "go to sleep" as a fixed phrase, which makes je vais dormir look like a word-for-word match. It is not: vais is the plan marker here, and "go to sleep" in the English sense would need a different verb entirely.
sentences.sound: dor-MEER, with both r's in the throat and the stress at the end, as always.

variations.display: Je vais dormir à la maison
variations.cue: I'm going to sleep at home
variations.changed: a place phrase behind the infinitive

variations.cue: Are you going to sleep?
variations.changed: allez and a rising voice, with the time phrase dropped

variations.display: Je ne vais pas dormir ce soir
variations.cue: I'm not going to sleep this evening
variations.changed: the brackets round vais, and the time phrase moved to the end

mistake.display: Ce soir je vais à dormir
mistake.why: Still no à between aller and the verb it plans: je vais dormir. English's "go to sleep" is what puts it there.

sentences.usage: The last plan of the day.
sentences.mnemonic: The gap after vais stays empty, whatever English does with its own "to".

sentences.display: Demain je vais faire du café
sentences.cue: Tomorrow I'm going to make coffee
sentences.literal: Tomorrow I go make of-the coffee

words.note: to make and to do at once — French does not split the two, so faire covers both English verbs and the choice a learner keeps trying to make simply is not there. Its participle, fait, was L1-M5's.

sentences.trap: An English speaker keeps looking for the second verb — the one that means "do" as against "make". There is not one. faire is both, and the sentence around it decides which English word fits.
sentences.sound: fair, one syllable, rhyming with the English "fair" but with the r in the throat.

variations.display: Demain je vais faire du thé
variations.cue: Tomorrow I'm going to make tea
variations.changed: swap the mass noun; the partitive is untouched by the plan

variations.cue: Are you going to make coffee?
variations.changed: allez and a rising voice

variations.cue: Yesterday I made coffee
variations.changed: the same verb pointed backwards — and its participle shares almost nothing with the bare form

mistake.display: Demain je vais fait du café
mistake.why: fait is the participle and belongs behind j'ai. After vais the verb is bare: faire.

sentences.usage: A plan to make or do something — the most useful verb in the module.
sentences.mnemonic: One French verb where English keeps two.
